extracted.intended_audience: general readers and scholars interested in film, media studies, and science communication
extracted.subtask_description: Critical analysis of the film Don't Look Up with emphasis on how it portrays science communication, political/media dynamics, representation, and satirical tone. Useful for students, critics, or scholars evaluating the film's themes and communicative strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Science communication is central to the film
rubrics_metrics.description: "The topic of science communication is at the forefront of the film, as it revolves around Mindy and Dibiasky, two scientists, struggling to share the news of their discovery with politicians, talk show hosts, and civilians who are ignorant about the scientific facts of humanity's impending destruction by Comet Dibiasky."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should consider how the film depicts scientists' efforts to communicate evidence to non‑experts, the obstacles they encounter (political, media, public ignorance), and how that depiction serves the film's themes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depiction of partisan divides, affective polarization, distrust toward science, and news media sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: As quoted from Journal of Science Communication (Niels G. Mede): "the film depicts sharp partisan divides, strong affective polarization, high distrust toward science within certain social milieus, and pronounced news media sensationalism, which have been found to be characteristic of the United States..."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the film accurately or effectively illustrates these social phenomena, and whether those depictions are treated as specifically American or more universal. Consider how partisan politics and sensationalist media behavior drive narrative and satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Does the film imagine alternatives / explain the cause? (centering marginalized voices vs privileging global north perspectives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Julie Doyle: "yet, as the film critiques existing structures and systems it does not imagine an alternative set of realities, nor explain the comet's cause. In focusing upon the fictional stories of scientists, politicians, and media celebrities, the film fails to center any marginalized voices, continuing to privilege global north perspectives, even as these are satirised."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A critique dimension is whether a work that indicts systems also offers alternatives or broader perspectives. Evaluators should note inclusivity of viewpoints (marginalized voices), whether global north biases remain, and whether the narrative provides structural context (e.g., causes, solutions) beyond satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Media training for scientists (style adaptation and simplifying communication)
rubrics_metrics.description: The article discusses media training as a solution depicted in the film: the Chief Editor proposes media training, and commentary notes: "The style that scientists use to communicate science to peer scientists is mostly objective, complex, and full of technical jargon, which is difficult for the general public to connect to—even if it is in the same language."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging the film's communication lessons, consider portrayals of media training techniques, the tension between technical accuracy and public accessibility, and whether the film endorses or problematizes training strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storytelling as a strategy to mitigate science skepticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Samer Angelone and Niels G. Mede note: "The film also illustrates that storytelling can be a promising strategy to mitigate these reservations ... showing how Mindy is advised before a TV interview that he is 'just telling a story' and must 'keep it simple.'"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this criterion to evaluate how effectively storytelling (simplification, narrative framing) is presented as a communication tool, and whether the film demonstrates trade‑offs between narrative appeal and scientific nuance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gendered norms and emotions affecting credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Julie Doyle: "Gendered norms affect Mindy and Dibiasky's public credibility and the mitigatory comet actions they promote. Following his own emotional outburst on TV, Mindy is subsequently recuperated through processes of celebritisation ... In contrast, Dibiasky is discredited and side‑lined from rational public commentary through (climate) memes."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess representation of gendered emotional expectations, how emotional expression influences public credibility, and the film's portrayal of celebritisation, marginalization, and online shaming/memes as gendered phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of historic figures/easter eggs to nuance science–politics relationship
rubrics_metrics.description: The film includes many historic figures as Easter eggs (e.g., Carl Sagan on Dibiasky's desk; juxtaposition with a painting of George W. Bush; an Oval Office portrait of Andrew Jackson) that comment on scientific credibility, political denialism, and populism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how references to real historic figures function thematically—whether they deepen critique, create allegory (e.g., Sagan as scientific credibility), or risk oversimplifying complex histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic imagery and allegory (e.g., Last Supper ending)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The film ends with a scene that reflects the Last Supper. Dr. Mindy, his family, Kate, Yule, and Teddy all sit around a dinner table and engage in a hand‑held prayer... moments later Comet Dibiasky destroys Earth."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the effectiveness of religious and symbolic imagery in reinforcing the film's themes about collective denial, ritual, and the human response to catastrophe.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone and balance between humor and satire (does humor undercut the message?)
rubrics_metrics.description: Referenced critiques in the article include comments like 'Broad humor undermines satire' and 'Scattershot Netflix satire' (reviews cited). The film is variously described as 'very funny, very depressing' and as balancing comedy with an apocalyptic message.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this evaluative dimension to judge whether the film's comedic elements strengthen or weaken its satirical critique and moral urgency—assess pacing, tonal consistency, and whether humor clarifies or distracts from the film's political/social commentary.
